content: Galanthus, commonly known as snowdrop, is a small genus of approximately 20 species of bulbous, herbaceous perennials belonging to the Amaryllis family. The name derives from the Greek words gála (milk) and ánthos (flower), referencing the white color of its flowers. Most species bloom in winter, prior to the vernal equinox, though some flower in early spring or late autumn. Snowdrops are often mistaken for related genera within the Galantheae tribe, such as Leucojum (snowflakes) and Acis. All Galanthus species are perennial plants that grow from bulbs. Each bulb typically produces two or three linear leaves and a single, erect, leafless flowering stalk (scape). At the top of the scape, there are two bract-like spathe valves joined by a papery membrane, from which a solitary, pendulous, bell-shaped white flower emerges. The flower lacks true petals and instead consists of six tepals, with the outer three being larger and more convex than the inner three. The six anthers open via pores or short slits, and the ovary is three-celled, maturing into a three-celled capsule. The seeds are whitish and possess a small, fleshy appendage (elaiosome) that attracts ants, aiding in seed dispersal. After flowering, the leaves die back within a few weeks. The inner segments of the flower are often marked with a green or greenish-yellow bridge-shaped marking near the notch (sinus) at the tip of each tepal. A key feature for distinguishing between species and identifying hybrid parentage is the vernation, or the arrangement of emerging leaves relative to one another. Vernation types include applanate (leaves pressed flat against each other), supervolute (one leaf tightly clasped around the other), and explicative (leaves pressed flat but with edges folded back or rolled). Notable species include: Galanthus nivalis (Common snowdrop): Grows 7–15 cm tall and flowers between January and April in the northern temperate zone. It exhibits applanate vernation. Galanthus plicatus (Crimean snowdrop): Reaches 30 cm in height, flowers from January to March, and has broad leaves folded back at the edges (explicative vernation). Galanthus elwesii (Giant snowdrop): Native to the Levant, grows to 23 cm tall, flowers in January and February, and features large flowers with prominent green blotches on the inner segments. It exhibits supervolute vernation. Galanthus reginae-olgae: Found in Greece and Sicily, it flowers in autumn before the leaves appear. The leaves, which emerge in spring, have a characteristic white stripe on their upper side. It exhibits applanate vernation. The genus Galanthus was established by Carl Linnaeus in 1753, with Galanthus nivalis as the type species. The name Galanthus reflects the milk-white color of the flowers, while nivalis means of the snow. Snowdrops are sometimes confused with related genera such as Leucojum and Acis. Leucojum species are larger, flower in spring or early summer, and have six tepals of equal size. Some Galanthus species with poculiform (goblet-shaped) flowers may resemble Leucojum. As of February 2012, the World Checklist of Selected Plant Families recognizes 19 species of Galanthus, with a 20th species, Galanthus panjutinii, identified in 2012. This species, found in a small area of the northern Colchis region (western Transcaucasus) of Georgia and Russia, is classified as endangered. One of its five known sites, located in Sochi, was destroyed during preparations for the 2014 Winter Olympics. The genus Galanthus is native to Europe and the Middle East, spanning from Spain, France, and Germany in the west to Iran in the east. It has become naturalized in parts of northern Europe, such as Norway, Sweden, and the British Isles, as well as in eastern Canada and the United States. Galanthus nivalis is the most widespread and well-known species, native to a broad area of Europe. Although often thought to be a native British wildflower, it was likely introduced to the British Isles in the early 16th century. Some Galanthus species are threatened in their natural habitats, and collecting bulbs from the wild is illegal in most countries. Under CITES regulations, international trade in Galanthus plants, bulbs, or even dead specimens is prohibited without a permit. Limited trade in wild-collected bulbs of three species (G. nivalis, G. elwesii, and G. woronowii) is allowed from Turkey and Georgia. Snowdrops are celebrated as a symbol of spring and can form striking carpets of white in areas where they are native or naturalized. Many gardens in the UK and Ireland open during snowdrop season to showcase these displays, attracting numerous visitors. Snowdrop enthusiasts, known as galanthophiles, often collect rare cultivars and hybrids, which can differ in flower size, shape, markings, and flowering period. Propagation of snowdrops is typically achieved through offset bulbs, either by dividing clumps during active growth (in the green) or after the leaves have withered. Seeds can also be sown when ripe or in spring. Advanced methods like twin-scaling are used by professionals to rapidly increase stocks of desirable cultivars. Galanthus contains active compounds such as galantamine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that has been used in the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease, though it is not a cure. Galantamine also occurs naturally in daffodils and other narcissi. Another active substance, Galanthus nivalis agglutinin (GNA), is a lectin with potential applications in genetic engineering. In 1995, Árpád Pusztai genetically modified potatoes with the GNA gene, sparking controversy over the safety of genetically modified organisms. In popular culture, snowdrops have appeared in various stories and traditions. For example, in the Russian fairy tale The Twelve Months, a young girl gathers snowdrops in winter with the help of the spirits of the months. Snowdrops were also nicknamed snowdrops by British citizens during World War II to describe the white-helmeted U.S. military police stationed in the UK.
